title: Systems, Linux, Windows & Networks
tagline: The machine, administered — Linux to RHCSA/RHCE, Windows Server, and networks with packet literacy.
blurb: IL-04 is the systems administration academy: Linux from first principles through the RHCSA EX200 performance exam (with LPIC as the vendor-neutral companion), Windows Server administration (identity, Group Policy, PowerShell), networking to Network+ N10-009 with Wireshark-level packet literacy, and RHCE EX294 Ansible automation. Performance exams are won in the terminal — every module pairs concept notes with original hands-on labs, timed troubleshooting scenarios, and a terminal simulator.

objectives: Administer Linux from first principles: filesystem, permissions, shell, systemd, storage, networking, SELinux.
Automate with bash and Ansible: idempotent playbooks, roles, and scheduled execution.
Administer Windows Server: NTFS, Active Directory, Group Policy, PowerShell, DNS/DHCP.
Troubleshoot networks by layer with packet-level evidence: addressing, switching, routing, wireless.
Pass performance exams (EX200/EX294) via timed hands-on scenarios — not multiple-choice cramming.

arc.title: First principles
arc.body: The shell as an instrument, the filesystem hierarchy, permissions, pipes and text processing. You learn to *think* in pipelines before you automate anything — because automation of a bad process just makes bad faster.

arc.title: Administration
arc.body: Users, systemd, storage (LVM/Stratis), networking, firewalls, SELinux on Linux; NTFS, AD, Group Policy, PowerShell on Windows. Two operating systems, one discipline: least privilege, documented change, verified state.

arc.title: Automation & proof
arc.body: Ansible playbooks and roles for RHCE; PBQ drills and timed scenarios for every performance exam. The exam is a workday compressed — you prepare by doing workdays.

modules.title: Linux Foundations to RHCSA
modules.summary: Welcome to IL-04 — Systems, Linux, Windows & Networks. I'm your instructor for this course, and this is Module 1: Linux Foundations to RHCSA. Over this module we take you from first principles — the shell as an instrument, the filesystem hierarchy, permissions — through real administration (users, systemd, LVM storage, firewalld, SELinux) and on to the RHCSA EX200 performance exam, with LPIC-1/LPIC-2 running alongside as the vendor-neutral companion track. Performance exams are won in the terminal: every concept below pairs with a hands-on lab, and you will break things and fix them under time. If you can think in pipelines, administer with least privilege, and read an SELinux denial without flinching, this module has done its job.
objectives: Navigate and manipulate the filesystem hierarchy with pipeline fluency.
Manage users, groups, ACLs, systemd services, LVM/Stratis storage, and firewalld.
Apply SELinux contexts and troubleshoot denials.
Work EX200-style timed tasks: the exam is a workday compressed.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **filesystem hierarchy** — the map of a Linux system: /etc holds configuration, /var holds variable data (logs, spool), /usr holds programs and libraries, /home holds user data, /proc and /sys are kernel interfaces, not real files.
- **permissions** — the law: rwx across user/group/other, expressed as octal (640 = rw-r-----), plus setuid/setgid/sticky bits (4755 = setuid + rwxr-xr-x: executes with the file owner's privileges).
- **pipes** — connect a command's stdout to the next command's stdin (|): the instrument you think in, as in journalctl ... | grep -i error | awk '{print $5}' | sort | uniq -c | sort -nr — filter, extract, count, rank.
- **redirection** — send output to files: > overwrites, >> appends.
- **text processing** — grep, sed, awk, sort, uniq, xargs: the toolkit for turning log noise into answers.
- **set -euo pipefail** — the three lines that prevent 3 AM pages: exit on error (-e), on undefined variables (-u), and on pipe failures (-o pipefail). In every script.
- **users/groups/ACLs** — useradd and groupmod manage identity; setfacl/getfacl grant fine-grained access beyond owner/group/other.
- **systemd** — the init and service manager: units with [Unit]/[Service]/[Install] sections, systemctl enable --now to enable and start, journalctl -u to read a service's logs, targets and timers (timers are the modern cron: calendar or monotonic triggers with journal logging).
- **LVM** — the layer that makes resizing sane: physical volumes (PV, the disks) pour into a volume group (VG, the pool); logical volumes (LV) are sliced out. Resize any layer independently; also Stratis, Btrfs, and VDO (deduplication/compression) as the storage alternatives.
- **firewalld** — zone-based firewalling: assign interfaces to zones, open services not ports (--add-service=http), rich rules for exceptions.
- **ip / nmcli / ss** — the modern networking tools: ip replaces ifconfig, nmcli manages NetworkManager, ss -tlnp shows TCP listening sockets with numeric ports and the owning process.
- **SELinux** — mandatory access control by context (user:role:type:level): a file can have correct Unix permissions and still be denied because its context is wrong. ls -Z shows contexts, restorecon repairs them, semanage fcontext persists the rule, audit2allow generates policy (use sparingly — understand the denial before allowing it).
- **podman** — daemonless, rootless container runtime: the RHEL-native tool (quadlets integrate containers with systemd as services).
- **RHCSA (EX200)** — Red Hat's hands-on performance exam: broken systems and a clock, man pages available; it recycles the same five root causes (service running? port listening? firewall? SELinux? disk full?).
- **LPIC-1 / LPIC-2** — the vendor-neutral Linux Professional Institute track (101/102 essentials, 201/202 advanced): the companion proof alongside the Red Hat one.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Do this on a lab VM or with loop devices — never on a machine you care about. The procedure builds the full LVM lifecycle and grows the filesystem online, then writes a hardening audit script.

1. Create a file-backed 'disk' so the lab is safe anywhere: dd if=/dev/zero of=/tmp/disk1.img bs=1M count=256, then DEV=$(losetup -f --show /tmp/disk1.img).
2. Build the LVM layers in order: pvcreate "$DEV", then vgcreate vgdata "$DEV", then lvcreate -n applv -L 100M vgdata.
3. Put a filesystem on it and mount it: mkfs.xfs /dev/vgdata/applv, mkdir -p /mnt/app, mount /dev/vgdata/applv /mnt/app; confirm with df -h /mnt/app.
4. Extend online with zero downtime: lvextend -L +100M /dev/vgdata/applv, then xfs_growfs /mnt/app (or resize2fs for ext4). Confirm the new size with df -h.
5. Clean up in reverse: umount, lvremove, vgremove, pvremove, losetup -d.
6. Write the hardening audit script starting every script with set -euo pipefail: grep -R NOPASSWD /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/ for passwordless sudo, find /etc -xdev -type f -perm -0002 for world-writable files, ss -tlnp for listening ports, and journalctl -u sshd --since today | grep -ci 'failed' for today's failed SSH logins; write all findings to a dated report file.
7. Create an SELinux trap on purpose: move a file from /home to /srv/web, confirm ls -Z shows the wrong context, then restorecon -Rv /srv/web and confirm the service can read it again. This is the exam's favorite trap — rehearse it until it is boring.
notes.code:
set -euo pipefail
dd if=/dev/zero of=/tmp/disk1.img bs=1M count=256
DEV=$(losetup -f --show /tmp/disk1.img)
pvcreate "$DEV" && vgcreate vgdata "$DEV" && lvcreate -n applv -L 100M vgdata
mkfs.xfs -f /dev/vgdata/applv && mount /dev/vgdata/applv /mnt/app
lvextend -L +100M /dev/vgdata/applv && xfs_growfs /mnt/app
ls -Z /srv/web/index.html        # check the context first
restorecon -Rv /srv/web          # fix the context
journalctl -u sshd --since today | grep -ci 'failed'

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body:
Your applied capstone for this module: deliver a hardened, documented RHEL 9 server build — the kind of hand-off a senior admin would accept without rework.

The scenario. A small company needs one RHEL 9 application server rebuilt from a kickstart: the old box failed its audit (world-writable configs, passwordless sudo entries, SELinux in permissive mode, services listening that nobody can explain).

Your deliverables:
- A build script (bash, set -euo pipefail) that creates the application LV on LVM, mounts it, sets ownership and permissions (640/750 discipline, umask 027 for the app user), and enables the services via systemd units — one of them on a systemd timer.
- The hardening audit script from the Hands-on procedure, run against your own build, with its findings report attached and every finding either remediated or documented with a reason.
- SELinux enforcing with correct contexts on all application paths (show ls -Z before/after for at least one relabeled path); firewalld allowing only the required services.
- A one-page operations note: how to extend the application volume online, where the logs live (journalctl), and the five-root-cause triage order for 'the app is down'.

Stretch: containerize the application with podman and manage it as a systemd service via a quadlet, rootless.

notes.title: Noah check-in
notes.body:
Noah probes mastery with questions like:
- Walk Noah through the exact layer order you would check when a service cannot read a file it could read yesterday: permissions, then context — why is that order correct?
- Give Noah the LVM layer order (PV -> VG -> LV) and explain why extending the filesystem without extending the LV first cannot work.
- *Timed drill:* Noah gives you a moved file with correct Unix permissions and a denied service. Name the two commands that diagnose and fix it, and say why setenforce 0 is the wrong answer.

Honesty note: all labs, scenarios, and questions in this module are original practice material — never recalled exam content. EX200 is a hands-on performance exam; confirm the current objectives on redhat.com before booking, because exam versions change. Preparation only: this course confers no certificate and is not affiliated with Red Hat or LPI.

cards.back: /etc: configuration. /var: variable data (logs, spool). /usr: programs and libraries.
setuid (4) + rwxr-xr-x: executes with the file owner's privileges.
PV (disks) → VG (pool) → LV (usable volumes). Resize any layer independently.

cards.front: SELinux denial with correct Unix perms: first check?
cards.back: ls -Z — the context is wrong. restorecon or semanage fcontext to fix.
Timers are systemd-native: logging via journal, dependencies, calendar or monotonic triggers. cron is simpler and universal.
TCP listening sockets with numeric ports and the owning process — the 'is it listening and who owns it' command.
New files 640 (rw-r-----), new directories 750 (rwxr-x---).
Grants user ana rwx on the file — fine-grained access beyond owner/group/other; verify with getfacl.

quiz.q: A service fails to read /srv/data/file after a move from /home. Permissions are correct. Likely cause?
quiz.explain: mv preserves the source context (/home) — restorecon -Rv /srv/data fixes it. Classic RHCSA trap. Covered in the Concepts section.

quiz.q: Which grows a filesystem online after extending its LV?
choices: resize2fs / xfs_growfs on the mounted fs
quiz.explain: LVM + online resize: lvextend then resize2fs (ext4) or xfs_growfs (XFS) — no downtime. Covered in the Hands-on procedure section.

quiz.q: firewalld: allow HTTP persistently?
quiz.explain: Zone model: --add-service=http --permanent, then reload. Services, not raw ports. Covered in the Concepts section.

quiz.q: set -euo pipefail guards against?
choices: silent failures: unchecked errors, unset vars, masked pipe failures
quiz.explain: -e exits on error, -u on unset variables, -o pipefail propagates pipe failures — the 3 AM page preventers. Covered in the Concepts section.

quiz.q: podman vs docker, RHEL exam relevance?
choices: podman: daemonless, rootless, quadlets for systemd — the RHEL-native tool
quiz.explain: EX200 tests podman: rootless containers managed as systemd services via quadlets. Covered in the Concepts section.

quiz.q: EX200 time strategy?
choices: read all, quick wins first, verify each, man pages allowed
quiz.explain: Triage like a workday: quick wins, flag long tasks, verify as you go, use man -k. Covered in the Noah check-in section.

quiz.q: A new deploy user needs default file permissions 640. What umask do you set in their profile?
quiz.explain: umask 027 strips write for group and all for other: new files 640, directories 750. Covered in the Project brief section.

quiz.q: You need to give contractor 'ana' read-write-execute on /srv/app without changing the owner or group. Command?
quiz.explain: setfacl grants per-user rights beyond owner/group/other; chmod 777 and group changes are over-broad. Covered in the Concepts section.

modules.title: Windows Systems Administration
modules.summary: Welcome back to IL-04 — Systems, Linux, Windows & Networks. I'm your instructor, and this is Module 2: Windows Systems Administration. Linux gave you the shell as an instrument; Windows gives you the other half of the enterprise: NTFS permissions and the effective-access rule, services and the registry, event logs and diagnostics — then identity with Active Directory (forests, domains, OUs, Group Policy, Kerberos and NTLM), PowerShell automation through the object pipeline, and the networking services Windows Server runs (DNS, DHCP, file and print). The discipline carries over: least privilege, documented change, verified state. By the end you will read a GPO conflict, a Kerberos failure, and a permission mystery the way you now read a pipeline — start to finish, with evidence at every step.
objectives: Apply NTFS vs share permissions correctly — and explain the effective-access rule.
Design AD structure: forests, domains, OUs; deploy Group Policy deliberately.
Automate with the PowerShell pipeline: filter left, format right.
Run DNS/DHCP/file services and troubleshoot with event logs.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **NTFS permissions** — file-system rights (Full Control, Modify, Read & Execute, List Folder Contents, Read, Write, plus special permissions like Traverse and Execute File): they travel with the file and form the real security boundary.
- **share permissions** — the network entry point's rights: they combine with NTFS, and the effective access is the *most restrictive* of the two. This single rule answers half the permissions questions.
- **effective access** — compute it, don't guess it: the Effective Access tab shows the real result; guessing permissions is how outages happen.
- **services** — background processes managed via services.msc, sc.exe, or PowerShell Get-Service: startup types, dependencies, and recovery actions.
- **registry** — the configuration database (e.g. HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services): export before editing, always.
- **event logs** — Event Viewer (System/Application/Security), wevtutil, Reliability Monitor: troubleshooting starts here. Methodology: reproduce, check logs, isolate, fix, verify, document.
- **Server Core vs Desktop Experience** — Core is the smaller attack surface with fewer patches: the exam's preferred answer for a new server, fully manageable remotely.
- **forest** — the Active Directory security boundary; contains domains, which contain OUs. Design OUs by *administration*, not by org chart.
- **Group Policy** — GPOs link to sites, domains, and OUs; processing order is LSDOU (Local, Site, Domain, OU — later wins); Enforced beats Block Inheritance. gpupdate /force applies now, gpresult /r shows what applied.
- **AGDLP** — the canonical group-nesting pattern: Accounts go into Global groups, into Domain Local groups, which get the Permissions.
- **Kerberos** — ticket-based authentication (AS then TGS then service): needs time sync (more than ~5 minutes of skew kills auth), registered SPNs, and a reachable KDC — the troubleshooting trio.
- **NTLM** — legacy challenge-response authentication: pass-the-hash risk, avoid where Kerberos works.
- **hybrid identity** — Entra ID Connect syncs on-prem AD with Entra ID for SSO shapes across cloud and on-prem.
- **PowerShell pipeline** — passes *objects*, not text: Get-Process | Where-Object CPU -gt 100 | Sort-Object CPU -Descending | Select-Object -First 5. Filter left (Where-Object early), format right (Format-* last — formatting destroys the objects).
- **PowerShell remoting / DSC** — Enter-PSSession and Invoke-Command run code on remote machines; DSC is the declarative configuration model (desired state, LCM enforces it).
- **DNS** — zones, records, forwarders, scavenging: internal resolution working but external failing points at forwarders or root hints first.
- **DHCP** — scopes, reservations, failover: the DORA dance (Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge); the classic 80/20 scope split is legacy thinking — proper failover is the modern answer.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Do this on a lab Server Core VM with the AD DS role — the procedure rehearses the three skills the module keeps testing: permissions reasoning, GPO scoping, and pipeline discipline.

1. Create a folder C:\Share\Finance, set NTFS Modify for the Finance group and share Read for the same group; then open the Effective Access tab for a Finance user and record the result: Read — most restrictive wins. Widen the share to Change and re-check.
2. Build the OU design: one OU per administration boundary (e.g. OU=Workstations,OU=Sales), never one OU per org-chart box. Link a GPO at the domain level and a conflicting setting at the OU level.
3. Run gpresult /r on a test client and read which GPO won the conflict: the OU-linked one (LSDOU — later wins). Then set Enforced on the domain GPO and re-check the flip.
4. Break Kerberos on purpose: skew the client clock by 8 minutes and attempt a domain logon; confirm failure. Sync with w32tm, confirm logon works. You now own the most-tested Windows troubleshooting fact there is.
5. Write a PowerShell audit one-liner and save it as a script (no aliases in scripts): Get-Service | Where-Object {$_.Status -eq 'Running'} | Sort-Object DisplayName | Select-Object Name, Status — filter left, format right.
6. Use Invoke-Command to run the audit against two lab machines at once: remoting is how one admin covers a fleet.
7. Document every change you made (GPO links, share/NTFS settings, clock skew) with a rollback note — documented change is the discipline, not the paperwork.
notes.code:
# Effective access: most restrictive of NTFS vs share wins
Get-SmbShareAccess -Name Finance
icacls C:\Share\Finance
# GPO scoping: what applied, and who won
gpupdate /force
gpresult /r
# Kerberos clock check
w32tm /query /status
# Pipeline discipline: filter left, format right
Get-Service | Where-Object {$_.Status -eq 'Running'} | Sort-Object DisplayName | Select-Object Name, Status
# One audit, many machines
Invoke-Command -ComputerName SRV1,SRV2 -ScriptBlock { Get-Service | Where-Object {$_.Status -eq 'Running'} }

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body:
Your applied capstone for this module: stand up a small, defensible Windows domain lab and hand over the runbook.

The scenario. A 25-person company has been running as a workgroup with 'everyone shares everything'. They have approved a single new domain controller — Server Core, because you argued the smaller attack surface — and one file server.

Your deliverables:
- The OU design document: forest/domain/OU layout designed by administration boundary, the AGDLP group-nesting plan for Finance, Sales, and IT, and where each GPO links (with the LSDOU reasoning written down, not assumed).
- Three working GPOs: a baseline security policy at the domain level, a mapped-drive/preferences GPO at the OU level (preferences where reversibility matters, policies where enforcement matters), and one Enforced setting with a written justification for why it overrides Block Inheritance risk.
- NTFS + share permission matrix for the company shares, each cell justified by the effective-access rule, and a screenshot-equivalent transcript of the Effective Access tab check per share.
- A PowerShell runbook script (pipeline-disciplined, no aliases): audit script that reports services, share permissions, and last GPO application across both servers via remoting, output as objects ready for Export-Csv.
- The Kerberos triage card: time sync, SPN, KDC reachability — the three checks, in order, with the commands.

Stretch: configure DHCP failover between the two servers and document the DORA flow you observed in a packet capture.

notes.title: Noah check-in
notes.body:
Noah probes mastery with questions like:
- A user has NTFS Full Control and Share Read on a folder. State their effective access and the rule that produces it — then explain why you would still set both deliberately instead of relying on one.
- Two GPOs conflict: one linked at the Domain, one at the OU, nothing enforced. Which wins, and what single change flips the outcome?
- *Hands-on:* Noah skews your lab client's clock by 10 minutes. Diagnose the logon failure out loud: which protocol broke, why, and the exact command that fixes it.

Honesty note: all labs, scenarios, and questions in this module are original practice material — never recalled exam content. Windows Server versions and PowerShell behaviors change: confirm against Microsoft Learn before treating any behavior as current. Preparation only: this course confers no certificate and is not affiliated with Microsoft.

cards.back: Most restrictive wins. NTFS Full + Share Read = Read.
LSDOU: Local → Site → Domain → OU. Later wins (unless Enforced/Block).
Time skew >5 min, missing SPN, KDC unreachable.
Accounts → Global groups → Domain Local groups → Permissions. The nesting pattern.
Objects, not text — hence Where-Object/Select-Object instead of grep/awk.
Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge — the four-packet lease dance.

cards.front: Why set BOTH NTFS and share permissions?
cards.back: NTFS is the real boundary (travels with the file); share is the network entry point. Set both deliberately; effective access is the most restrictive of the two.
Preferences tattoo lightly (reversible, user can change); policies enforce (reapply, locked). Use preferences where reversibility matters.

quiz.q: NTFS Modify + Share Read on a folder. User's effective access?
quiz.explain: Most restrictive of NTFS and share wins: Read. Covered in the Concepts section.

quiz.q: A GPO linked at Domain and OU conflict. Which wins (no enforcement)?
quiz.explain: LSDOU — later (closer to the object) wins; OU beats Domain. Covered in the Concepts section.

quiz.q: Kerberos fails across the domain; clocks differ by 8 minutes. Fix?
quiz.explain: Kerberos tolerates ~5 min skew — 8 minutes breaks ticket validation. Sync time first. Covered in the Hands-on procedure section.

quiz.q: Pipeline best practice?
choices: filter with Where-Object early, format last
quiz.explain: Filter left (reduce objects early), format right (formatting destroys the objects). Covered in the Concepts section.

quiz.q: DNS resolves internally but not externally. Check first?
quiz.explain: Internal resolution works → the server is fine; external failure points at forwarders/root hints. Covered in the Concepts section.

quiz.q: Server Core vs Desktop Experience for a new DC?
choices: Core — smaller attack surface, fewer patches
quiz.explain: Core is the exam's preferred answer: less surface, fewer reboots, fully manageable remotely. Covered in the Concepts section.

quiz.q: In AGDLP, which group type receives the permission directly?
quiz.explain: Accounts → Global → Domain Local → Permissions: the Domain Local group is the one stamped with the permission. Covered in the Concepts section.

quiz.q: Why prefer Kerberos over NTLM where both are available?
choices: NTLM carries pass-the-hash risk; Kerberos is ticket-based and stronger
quiz.explain: NTLM is legacy challenge-response with pass-the-hash risk; Kerberos tickets are the modern, stronger mechanism. Covered in the Concepts section.

modules.title: Networking Core: Network+
modules.summary: Welcome to Module 3 of IL-04 — Systems, Linux, Windows & Networks. I'm your instructor, and this module is the network itself: the Network+ N10-009 core with Wireshark-level packet literacy. We start with the maps — the OSI and TCP/IP models, IPv4 and IPv6 addressing — then build the reflex every network engineer owns: subnetting to the point where a /27 is arithmetic, not a puzzle. From there: switching and VLANs, routing protocols, wireless, the appliances that sit in the path, and finally the skill that separates engineers from guessers — reading packets and applying the 6-step troubleshooting methodology with evidence. The Network+ exam leans on performance-based questions; this module rehearses exactly those, and the packet work you do here will serve every role you ever take after it.
objectives: Subnet IPv4 to reflex; explain IPv6 addressing structure.
Describe switching (VLANs, trunking) and routing (static, OSPF, BGP at concept level).
Read packets in Wireshark: identify handshakes, DNS, DHCP, TLS negotiation.
Apply the 6-step methodology to layered troubleshooting scenarios.
Beat Network+ PBQs: subnetting sims, CLI analysis, diagram troubleshooting.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **OSI model** — seven layers (physical → data link → network → transport → session → presentation → application): the troubleshooting map. Isolate bottom-up — cabling before configuration.
- **TCP/IP model** — the four-layer working model the Internet actually runs on; OSI is the map, TCP/IP is the territory.
- **IPv4 / CIDR** — dotted-decimal addresses with prefix lengths: /24 = 254 hosts, /27 = 30 hosts, hosts = 2^(32-n) − 2.
- **IPv6** — hex addresses with prefix lengths; no broadcast (multicast instead); link-local fe80::/10, global unicast, and subnetting on nibble boundaries (/48 site, /64 subnet) — easier than v4 once the hex clicks.
- **subnetting** — borrowing host bits to carve networks: the 60-second drill (given any /25–/28, produce network/broadcast/usable range) is trainable and tested.
- **VLSM** — variable-length subnet masks: right-size each subnet (point-to-point links get /30 or /31, VLANs get what they need) instead of wasting a /24 on two routers.
- **summarization** — aggregating contiguous blocks (192.168.0.0/24 through 192.168.3.0/24 → 192.168.0.0/22): smaller routing tables, valid when the blocks are contiguous with the same next hop.
- **VLAN** — virtual LAN: segments broadcast domains on one switch fabric.
- **802.1Q** — the VLAN tagging standard: trunk ports carry tagged frames for multiple VLANs; access ports carry one untagged VLAN.
- **STP** — Spanning Tree Protocol: loop prevention. A port in blocking state is listening, not forwarding — that is the protocol working, not a failure.
- **OSPF** — link-state routing inside one autonomous system: Dijkstra's algorithm, areas, fast convergence.
- **BGP** — path-vector, the Internet's routing protocol: carries policy between autonomous systems (AS_PATH in concept). Different job from OSPF — interior speed vs exterior policy.
- **802.11 / wireless** — a/b/g/n/ac/ax across 2.4/5/6 GHz with MIMO and channel width; on 2.4 GHz only channels 1, 6, 11 don't overlap — the most-tested wireless fact in existence.
- **WPA2 vs WPA3** — WPA3's SAE handshake replaces the crackable WPA2 4-way handshake and resists offline dictionary attacks.
- **firewall** — stateful vs NGFW (next-generation, application-aware): the policy enforcement point.
- **load balancer** — distributes traffic across servers (algorithms: round-robin, least-connections).
- **proxy / IDS/IPS** — proxies mediate and cache; IDS detects, IPS prevents — placement determines what they can see.
- **SNMP / NetFlow/sFlow** — monitoring: SNMP polls device state, NetFlow/sFlow sample traffic. You can't troubleshoot what you don't measure — baselines first, anomaly detection second.
- **Wireshark** — the packet analyzer: follow a TCP stream, read the three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), spot retransmissions (congestion or loss), decode DNS and DHCP exchanges, recognize the TLS ClientHello.
- **6-step troubleshooting methodology** — identify the problem, establish a theory, test the theory, establish a plan, implement, verify and document. Same discipline as the scenarios: scope first (one host? one VLAN? everyone?), then bottom-up.
- **PBQ** — performance-based questions: Network+ sims for subnetting, CLI-output analysis, and diagram troubleshooting. The drill set rehearses exactly these; the objective weights say troubleshooting (24%) comes first.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Two drills, daily for two weeks. This is arithmetic reflex and packet reading — both are trained, not studied.

1. Subnetting drill: take 192.168.20.64/27. Host bits = 5, so 32 addresses: .64–.95. Network .64, broadcast .95, usable .65–.94. Do one random /25–/28 per day and time yourself; under 60 seconds is the target.
2. Summarization drill: take 10.1.0.0/24 through 10.1.3.0/24 — four contiguous /24s share 22 network bits → 10.1.0.0/22. Say the rule out loud: contiguous blocks, same next hop.
3. Open Wireshark on your lab interface and capture while you open one web page. Stop the capture.
4. Find the TCP three-way handshake: filter tcp.flags.syn==1, confirm the SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK sequence to the web server's port 443. That sequence is the most-read pattern in packet analysis.
5. Right-click one TCP packet and choose Follow → TCP Stream. Read the TLS ClientHello — the moment encryption negotiation begins.
6. Run a DHCP exchange (ipconfig /release then /renew on Windows, or restart networking on Linux) while capturing: identify the DORA sequence — Discover, Offer, Request, Acknowledge — four packets, in order.
7. Introduce loss on purpose (unplug for two seconds mid-transfer, or throttle the lab link) and watch retransmissions appear: retransmissions mean segments went unacknowledged — loss, congestion, or a dead peer.
8. Apply the 6-step methodology to one real lab fault per week: identify (scope: one host? one VLAN? everyone?), theory, test, plan, implement, verify/document. Write the one-paragraph postmortem.
notes.code:
# Subnetting reflex: /27 -> 32 addresses
# 192.168.20.64/27: network .64, broadcast .95, usable .65-.94
# Summarization: 10.1.0.0/24-10.1.3.0/24 -> 10.1.0.0/22
# Wireshark display filters for the drills:
tcp.flags.syn==1          # find handshakes
dns                      # DNS query/response pairs
bootp                    # DHCP DORA exchange
tcp.analysis.retransmission  # spot loss/congestion

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body:
Your applied capstone for this module: a network design document and a troubleshooting playbook for a small company — the two artifacts that prove you can both build and fix.

The scenario. A 60-person company is moving into a two-floor office: wired workstations, a small server room, warehouse scanners on Wi-Fi, and a guest network that must never touch the corporate LAN. Their current 'network' is one flat /24 and a consumer router.

Your deliverables:
- The addressing plan: VLSM design with right-sized subnets per VLAN (workstations, servers, voice, warehouse Wi-Fi, guest, and /30 or /31 point-to-point links), plus the summarized route you would advertise upstream — every subnet justified, no wasted space.
- The switching design: VLAN assignments, which ports are access vs 802.1Q trunk, where STP is protecting you, and the channel plan for the 2.4 GHz warehouse coverage (1/6/11, with the reasoning).
- The routing call: where static routes suffice and where a dynamic protocol earns its keep — OSPF inside, and the one-paragraph explanation of what BGP would be for if they ever multi-home.
- The security layer: firewall placement and policy sketch, where IDS/IPS sits, WPA3 for corporate wireless with the SAE rationale, and the guest segmentation that keeps visitors off the LAN.
- The troubleshooting playbook: the 6-step methodology written as a runbook ('the network is down' → scope first: one host? one VLAN? everyone?), the Wireshark capture procedure with the three patterns to check first (handshake, DNS, DHCP), and the monitoring baseline (what SNMP/NetFlow would collect so the next fault has something to compare against).

Stretch: produce the summarized supernet for a second site and show the single route entry that covers both.

- In a capture, Noah points at a burst of TCP retransmissions. What do they indicate, and what is the one thing they do NOT indicate?
- *Whiteboard:* Noah asks you to place OSPF and BGP on a two-site diagram and justify each placement in one sentence per protocol.

N10-009 domains and weights change: confirm the current objectives on comptia.org before booking. Preparation only: this course confers no certificate and is not affiliated with CompTIA.

cards.back: Physical → data link → network → transport → session → presentation → application. Cabling before configuration.
32 - 2 = 30. (/27 = 5 host bits = 32 addresses.)
802.1Q — trunk ports carry tagged frames for multiple VLANs.
OSPF: link-state, inside one AS, fast convergence. BGP: path-vector, between ASes, policy-driven.
1, 6, 11. Everything else overlaps.
SYN → SYN-ACK → ACK. Retransmissions in a capture mean loss/congestion.
Right-size each subnet with different masks (/30 for point-to-point, larger for VLANs) instead of one mask everywhere.
SNMP polls device state (up/down, counters); NetFlow/sFlow samples traffic flows. State vs traffic.

quiz.explain: Blocking prevents loops; the port listens but doesn't forward user traffic. Covered in the Concepts section.

modules.title: RHCE: Ansible Automation
modules.summary: Welcome to Module 4 of IL-04 — Systems, Linux, Windows & Networks. I'm your instructor, and this final module is where administration becomes engineering: Red Hat Certified Engineer EX294, Ansible automation on RHEL. This module assumes you can already administer the systems you're automating — a current RHCSA is required, because the exam tests *how* you automate what you already know how to configure by hand. We build the discipline from the ground up: inventory and patterns, playbooks and plays, variables and facts, idempotence as the definition of correct automation — then roles and Galaxy, the RHEL system roles, automation controller concepts, and timed performance scenarios under the clock. If your playbook runs twice with zero changes the second time, you are thinking like an automation engineer.
objectives: Write idempotent playbooks: inventory, plays, variables, facts, handlers.
Build roles; consume Galaxy and the RHEL system roles.
Reason about automation controller concepts: jobs, inventories, credentials.
Complete EX294-style timed scenarios: multi-system configuration under the clock.

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **inventory** — the list of managed hosts: INI or YAML, organized into groups; the exam starts here, so a wrong inventory fails everything downstream.
- **patterns** — host selection expressions: webservers:&staging intersects, webservers:!staging excludes, --limit narrows a run to one host for iteration.
- **playbook / play / task / module** — a playbook is a YAML list of plays; a play maps tasks onto hosts; a task calls a module. Ad-hoc first (ansible web -m ping) to prove the concept, then write the playbook.
- **variables and facts** — variables parameterize playbooks (extra vars with -e win every precedence fight); ansible_facts (e.g. ansible_facts['os_family']) describe the target for when: conditionals — one playbook, many distributions.
- **Jinja2** — the templating language inside playbooks: when: already evaluates Jinja2, so never double-wrap {{ }} inside a when: clause.
- **idempotence** — running twice changes nothing the second time: the *definition* of correct automation. Every task must be safe to re-run — state: present, never shell commands that append blindly.
- **handlers** — tasks that run once at the end of a play, only when notified by a changed task (notify: restart nginx): restart the service only when the config changed.
- **ansible-vault** — encrypts secrets at rest in the repo; decrypt at runtime with --ask-vault-pass or a vault password file. Never commit plaintext credentials.
- **roles** — reusable automation units with a conventional layout (tasks/main.yml, handlers/main.yml, templates/, defaults/main.yml): learn the layout once, reuse forever.
- **Galaxy** — the community sharing hub for roles: vet what you download.
- **RHEL system roles** — Red Hat's supported roles (timesync, selinux, firewall, storage, network): idempotent and tested — prefer them over hand-rolled or random Galaxy roles on the exam.
- **automation controller** — the enterprise scheduling and access layer over Ansible: know at concept level what a job template bundles (project + inventory + credentials + playbook), plus workflows and RBAC.
- **become** — privilege escalation done right: become: true on the play or task that needs root on the remotes.
- **EX294** — the RHCE performance exam: real RHEL systems and a clock, configured with Ansible to a specification. YAML indentation, Jinja2 quoting in when:, and a forgotten become: true are the common traps; --check --diff is the pre-flight for every run.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Build the idempotent web tier from the module lab, then prove idempotence — the proof is the grade.

1. Write the inventory first: a [web] group with your lab hosts. Run ansible web -m ping and confirm every host answers before writing a single task.
2. Skeleton the playbook before filling tasks: play name, hosts: web, become: true, empty tasks and handlers blocks, variable file if you need one. Structure first, logic second — this is the exam time-saver.
3. Add the package task with ansible.builtin.dnf: name=nginx, state=present. Declarative state, not shell commands.
4. Add the config task with ansible.builtin.template: src=index.html.j2, dest with mode '0644', and notify: restart nginx — the handler fires only when the template actually changes.
5. Add the firewall task with ansible.posix.firewalld: service=http, permanent=true, immediate=true, state=enabled. Services, not raw ports — same discipline as Module 1.
6. Add the service task with ansible.builtin.service: name=nginx, state=started, enabled=true.
7. Pre-flight: ansible-playbook web.yml --check --diff --limit web1 — the dry run shows what WOULD change, on one host.
8. Run for real: ansible-playbook web.yml. Then run it again immediately: the second run must report 0 changed. Zero changes on re-run is idempotence proven — that is the verdict you want.
9. Break it on purpose: change one line in the template, re-run, and confirm the handler fires exactly once and only the config task reports changed.
notes.code:
---
- name: web tier
  hosts: web
  become: true
  tasks:
    - name: nginx installed
      ansible.builtin.dnf:
        name: nginx
        state: present
    - name: index deployed
      ansible.builtin.template:
        src: index.html.j2
        dest: /usr/share/nginx/html/index.html
        mode: '0644'
      notify: restart nginx
    - name: http allowed
      ansible.posix.firewalld:
        service: http
        permanent: true
        immediate: true
        state: enabled
    - name: nginx running
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: nginx
        state: started
        enabled: true
  handlers:
    - name: restart nginx
      ansible.builtin.service:
        name: nginx
        state: restarted
# prove it:
ansible-playbook web.yml --check --diff --limit web1
ansible-playbook web.yml && ansible-playbook web.yml  # second run: 0 changed

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body:
Your applied capstone for this module: a timed, multi-system automation engagement — the closest rehearsal to EX294 short of the exam itself.

The scenario. A company has four RHEL systems fresh off the Module 1 build procedure and a specification document: two web servers behind one load-balancer config, one database server with a tuned config, and one monitoring host collecting logs — all to be brought to spec with Ansible, nothing by hand.

Your deliverables:
- The inventory with groups (web, db, monitor) and group variables; ad-hoc proof (ansible all -m ping) captured before any playbook ran.
- One playbook per tier, each starting from the skeleton-first pattern, using become: true where privilege is needed, handlers for every service restart, and when: conditionals on ansible_facts where the tiers diverge.
- At least one RHEL system role used where it fits (timesync across all four hosts is the natural one) instead of a hand-rolled equivalent — with the written reason.
- Secrets handled with ansible-vault (the database password), with the vault password file outside the repo and the encryption proven by showing the ciphertext in version control.
- The idempotence proof: two consecutive full runs with the second reporting 0 changed, plus the --check --diff pre-flight output for the final run.
- A time-boxed run log: you get one 90-minute window to go from empty repo to green second run — log start/end times and where the minutes went, because the exam is a workday compressed.

Stretch: convert the most-reused tier into a proper role (tasks/handlers/templates/defaults layout) and consume it from a thin wrapper playbook.

notes.title: Noah check-in
notes.body:
Noah probes mastery with questions like:
- Noah shows you a task using shell: echo x >> /etc/motd. Rule it idempotent or not, and rewrite it the idempotent way.
- Your playbook ran green but a re-run reports changes every time. Noah asks: what class of bug is this, and what is the first thing you check?
- *Timed:* Noah hands you a three-host spec and starts a 20-minute clock. Narrate your skeleton-first order of operations before you touch the keyboard.

Honesty note: all labs, scenarios, and questions in this module are original practice material — never recalled exam content. EX294 objectives and the required RHCSA version change: confirm the current spec on redhat.com before booking. Preparation only: this course confers no certificate and is not affiliated with Red Hat.

cards.back: Running twice changes nothing the second time. The definition of correct automation.
Only when a notifying task reports 'changed' — e.g., restart nginx only if the config changed.
Extra vars (-e) beat everything. Know the order for debugging surprises.
System roles are Red Hat-supported (timesync, selinux, firewall...) — prefer them on the exam.
Dry run showing what WOULD change — the pre-flight for every playbook run.
when: ansible_facts['os_family'] == 'RedHat' — no {{ }} wrapping; when: already evaluates Jinja2.
Conditionals (when:) — one playbook behaving correctly across distributions.
Project + inventory + credentials + playbook — the executable unit in automation controller.

quiz.q: A task using shell: echo x >> /etc/motd is ___.
choices: not idempotent — appends on every run
quiz.explain: >> appends every run — use copy/template with content: for idempotence. Covered in the Concepts section.

quiz.q: Restart nginx only when its config changed: mechanism?
quiz.explain: notify: restart nginx on the config task; the handler runs once, only on change. Covered in the Concepts section.

quiz.q: Target webservers except staging: pattern?
quiz.explain: ! excludes — webservers:&staging would intersect instead. Covered in the Concepts section.

quiz.q: Secrets in a playbook: correct handling?
quiz.explain: ansible-vault encrypts at rest; decrypt at runtime with --ask-vault-pass or a vault password file. Covered in the Concepts section.

quiz.q: Task needs root on remotes: add?
quiz.explain: become: true (privilege escalation) — the modern, correct directive. Covered in the Concepts section.

quiz.q: Playbook ran green but changed nothing on re-run: verdict?
quiz.explain: Zero changes on re-run is the goal — that's idempotence proven. Covered in the Noah check-in section.

quiz.q: Your when: clause is when: "{{ ansible_facts['os_family'] == 'RedHat' }}". What happens?
choices: breaks — when: already evaluates Jinja2, never double-wrap {{ }}
quiz.explain: when: evaluates Jinja2 natively; wrapping in {{ }} is the classic trap. Covered in the Concepts section.

quiz.q: You want to iterate a playbook against one host before the fleet. Flag?
quiz.explain: --limit narrows the run to one host; combine with --check --diff for the pre-flight. Covered in the Hands-on procedure section.

scriptLabs.title: LVM: Build, Extend, Grow — Online
scriptLabs.brief: Script the full LVM lifecycle: PV → VG → LV → filesystem → extend → online grow. Use loop devices so it's safe anywhere. Required fragments force the layer order.
scriptLabs.starter:
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
# Use a file-backed loop device as our 'disk'
dd if=/dev/zero of=/tmp/disk1.img bs=1M count=256
DEV=$(losetup -f --show /tmp/disk1.img)
echo "disk: $DEV"
# TODO: pvcreate, vgcreate vgdata, lvcreate -n applv -L 100M, mkfs.xfs, mount, then extend + xfs_growfs
scriptLabs.hint: pvcreate $DEV && vgcreate vgdata $DEV && lvcreate -n applv -L 100M vgdata && mkfs.xfs /dev/vgdata/applv. Extend: lvextend -L +100M /dev/vgdata/applv && xfs_growfs /mnt/app.
scriptLabs.solution:
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
dd if=/dev/zero of=/tmp/disk1.img bs=1M count=256
DEV=$(losetup -f --show /tmp/disk1.img)
pvcreate "$DEV"
vgcreate vgdata "$DEV"
lvcreate -n applv -L 100M vgdata
mkfs.xfs -f /dev/vgdata/applv
mkdir -p /mnt/app && mount /dev/vgdata/applv /mnt/app
df -h /mnt/app
# online extend: no unmount, no downtime
lvextend -L +100M /dev/vgdata/applv
xfs_growfs /mnt/app
df -h /mnt/app
# cleanup: umount /mnt/app; lvremove -y /dev/vgdata/applv; vgremove -y vgdata; pvremove -y $DEV; losetup -d $DEV

scriptLabs.title: Bash Hardening Audit Script
scriptLabs.brief: Write an audit script with set -euo pipefail that checks: passwordless sudo entries, world-writable files in /etc, listening ports without a known service, and failed SSH logins today. Output a findings report.
scriptLabs.starter:
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
REPORT=/tmp/audit-$(date +%F).txt
{
echo "=== hardening audit $(date) ==="
# TODO 1: sudoers without password (visudo -c friendly: grep NOPASSWD /etc/sudoers*)
# TODO 2: world-writable under /etc
# TODO 3: listening TCP ports (ss -tlnp)
# TODO 4: failed SSH logins today (journalctl)
} > "$REPORT"
echo "wrote $REPORT"
scriptLabs.hint: grep -R NOPASSWD /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/. find /etc -xdev -type f -perm -0002. journalctl -u sshd --since today | grep -i 'failed'.
scriptLabs.solution:
#!/bin/bash
set -euo pipefail
REPORT=/tmp/audit-$(date +%F).txt
{
echo "=== hardening audit $(date) ==="
echo '--- NOPASSWD sudoers ---'
grep -R --include='*' 'NOPASSWD' /etc/sudoers /etc/sudoers.d/ 2>/dev/null || echo 'none found'
echo '--- world-writable in /etc ---'
find /etc -xdev -type f -perm -0002 -print 2>/dev/null || echo 'none found'
echo '--- listening TCP ---'
ss -tlnp
echo '--- failed SSH today ---'
journalctl -u sshd --since today 2>/dev/null | grep -ci 'failed' || echo 0
} > "$REPORT"
echo "wrote $REPORT"

scenarios.title: The Website Is Down
scenarios.context: Monitoring: https://shop.example.com down. One web server, RHEL 9, nginx, behind firewalld.

options.why: Is the service running and listening? Two commands answer the first hypothesis in seconds.
Rebooting destroys evidence and the cause returns. Diagnose first.
One site down on one server is not an ISP outage — scope says local.
Local curl isolates the app from the network; firewall check isolates the network from the app.
It's running and listening — reinstalling a working service is superstition.

steps.prompt: Local curl works; external fails; firewall shows https allowed. Next?

options.text: Check SELinux: ausearch -m avc -ts recent; ls -Z on webroot
options.why: Service running + firewall open + local works = the classic SELinux denial pattern on external paths.
Never. Find the denial, fix the context, keep the firewall.

scenarios.title: Nobody Can Log In
scenarios.context: Monday 9 AM: domain logons failing across the site. DCs are up.

options.text: Time sync: w32tm /query /status on DC and client
options.why: Kerberos dies past ~5 min skew — and Monday-morning mass failure after a weekend NTP outage is the classic.
Mass password resets for an infrastructure fault punishes users for a server problem.

options.text: dcdiag + check SYSVOL/NETLOGON shares and DNS SRV records
options.why: dcdiag finds DC health issues; logon needs DNS SRV records and SYSVOL — verify the infrastructure.
The nuclear option for a diagnosis you haven't done. Never.

blocks.body: systemctl is-active <svc> → ss -tlnp (listening?) → firewall-cmd --list-all → ls -Z (SELinux?) → journalctl -u <svc> --since '10 min ago' → df -h (disk?)
chmod 640/750/644 · chown user:group · setfacl -m u:ana:rwx · getfacl · umask 027 → new files 640/750
pvcreate → vgcreate → lvcreate → mkfs → mount · extend: lvextend -r (auto-grows fs on some) or lvextend + resize2fs/xfs_growfs
getenforce · ls -Z · restorecon -Rv · semanage fcontext -a -t httpd_sys_content_t '/srv/web(/.*)?' · ausearch -m avc -ts recent
systemctl enable --now · systemctl status · journalctl -u <svc> -f · timers: OnCalendar=daily

answerBank.a: RHCSA if you want Red Hat-shop jobs (it's a performance exam — the strongest signal). LPIC-1 as the vendor-neutral companion; the overlap is ~60%, so the second costs little. This module prepares both in one pass.

answerBank.q: How do I beat SELinux instead of disabling it?
answerBank.a: Learn the three commands: ls -Z (see the context), restorecon (fix file contexts), semanage fcontext (persist the rule). Disabling SELinux on the exam fails the task; in production it removes a layer. The module's labs make contexts routine.

answerBank.q: NTFS or share permissions — which do I set?
answerBank.a: Both, deliberately: NTFS for the real security boundary (it travels with the file), share for the network entry point. Effective access is the most restrictive of the two — design with that rule, verify with the Effective Access tab.

answerBank.q: How do I get fast at subnetting?
answerBank.a: The 60-second drill in the trainer: random /25–/28, produce network/broadcast/usable range. Daily for two weeks. It's arithmetic reflex, not intelligence — everyone who practices gets fast.
You need lab time — containers or a VM with RHEL (developer subscription is free for individuals). The module's timed scenarios assume a lab; reading about Ansible doesn't pass EX294.

answerBank.q: Wireshark feels overwhelming — where to start?
answerBank.a: Three patterns: the TCP handshake (SYN/SYN-ACK/ACK), DNS query/response, DHCP DORA. Follow one TCP stream per session. The module's packet notes build from these three outward.
